title: Goldkette's band and merging technique with soul
summary: Of the white dance bands, Jean Goldkette's impressed him most; Waters argues he studied more than most Black musicians of the time and always aimed to blend technique with soul.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: While you were in Boston, were you aware of through records or through in-person appearances any of the more popular white dance orchestras - the Benson Orchestra of Chicago -

Yeah, I liked, at that time I enjoyed the Elk [?], very much those bands for their musical ability. But I tell you, I was still advanced, you know, I was still thinkin' advanced. Now of all those bands that I heard, the band, white band that knocked me out the most was Jean Goldkette's Band. And as you all know Jean Goldkette's Band was way ahead of bands like Benson, if you listen to the records. I won't say better, but way ahead, advanced. 'Cause I swear, I'm always thinkin' advanced. I always listened to things, the things that knocked me out was the ones that was more advanced all the time.

Do you feel you were more a part of - in your own time as opposed to your own heart - that you were perhaps more aligned than most of the black musicians of that time with the sound that was putting an emphasis on a cleaner technique playing -

Well, I don't want to be egotistic, but I thinks yes. I mean, and the reason for it, I think I studied more at that period than many other black musicians. I mean I think that was the cause, I think that was the trouble with the Negro musician - they didn't study early enough in that period, wherein the white musician been studying ever since he were born, you understand what I mean, see? I think so - not now, now the guys studyin' like son-of-a-gun, but I mean at that period.
view yourself as one of the first fusings of these two distinct principles of American music?
What d'you, I don't understand that -
Fusing, you know, put, blending together the emphasis on technique and the emphasis on soul, tryin' to tie the two together. Are you one of the first -
No, I would, no, no, I wouldn't say that, not soul. Because that soul, I mean the musicians had way from the very beginning, Negro musicians -
No, but I'm saying, the blending of them together, there's this technique tradition -
Well, I wouldn't say I'm the one of the first, but I would say that has always been my idea from the very beginning. And I do it better now than ever in my life.
